title: Householder happiness
hook: to Dighajanu: effort, protection, good friends, balanced living

segments.voice: Yesterday: the eight winds, gain and loss among them, and your line, let the wind blow past. Today, a man asks about gain and loss of the most practical kind: money.

Dighajanu, a layman of the Koliyan people, is honest about his situation. We're householders, he tells the Buddha. We live with wives and children, we use sandalwood, we wear garlands, we handle gold and silver. Teach us something that will bring us happiness in this life, and in the next. He isn't asking how to leave the world, but how to live in it well. And the Buddha, whom people sometimes imagine as a teacher of monks only, gives him a plain, practical answer, starting with work and money.
screen: `A LAYMAN NAMED DIGHAJANU.` → `WIVES, CHILDREN, GOLD.` → `HOW DO WE LIVE WELL?`

segments.voice: For happiness in this life, the Buddha says, four things. First, effort: being skilled and diligent in your work, whether farming, trading, herding or serving the king. Second, protection: guarding what you've honestly earned, so it isn't lost to theft, fire, flood or careless heirs. Third, good friends: spending time with people who are wise, generous and steady, and learning from them. Fourth, balanced living, with a picture. A goldsmith or his apprentice holds up a pair of scales and knows: this much has tipped it down, this much has tipped it up. In the same way, a householder knows what comes in and what goes out, and lives so that income exceeds spending, but not by hoarding. The sutta names both errors. Live too lavishly, and people say you're eating your wealth like a fig-eater; the old commentary pictures someone shaking a fig tree, knocking most of the fruit to the ground to eat a few. Live too stingily, and they say you'll die like a starving man. Then it names four drains on a fortune: chasing other people's spouses, drinking, gambling and bad friends. And then the other half. For happiness in the next life, four more: faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom, the same four that kept Nakula's parents together. Money advice and spiritual advice sit in one discourse, side by side, like the two pans of the scale.
screen: `EFFORT IN YOUR WORK.` · `PROTECT WHAT YOU EARN.` · `GOOD FRIENDS.` · then, large: `BALANCED LIVING.`

segments.voice: Picture the goldsmith's scale, two pans and a little needle, and bring to mind one account in your life: money, or time, energy, attention. Read it without judgment, what's coming in, what's going out, which way the needle leans. Then imagine one small adjustment, a grain added here or taken there, and feel the needle settle toward the middle.
Householder happiness. The Buddha's four for this life, effort, protection, good friends and balanced living, and four for the next: faith, virtue, generosity, wisdom. Today's word.
Your line: balanced living. Neither the fig-eater nor the starving man. Day six hundred seventy, done.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often cite the Dighajanu Sutta, sometimes called the Vyagghapajja Sutta, when speaking about work, money and family life, as the Buddha's counsel for lay people.

fork.setup: you're a householder with a family and a business. what does the Buddha tell you brings happiness in this life?
options: give away everything and become a monk.
effort, protecting your earnings, good friends, balanced living.
pray for good luck in business.
fork.reveal: four practical things, and then four more for the next life. he answers the householder as a householder.

original.note: Pali samajivikata: 'even living,' balanced living, spending in proportion to income.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism only cares about giving things up.
what it means: the Buddha told a family man how to earn, protect and balance his wealth.
what a scholar hears: the man's name, Dighajanu, means 'long-knee'; the sutta is also called Vyagghapajja, after his clan's name.

chat.says: Did the Buddha ever give advice about money, or only about giving it up?
options: He told Dighajanu: work well, protect your earnings, keep good friends, and balance in and out.
Only to give it up; he said a householder's money always stands in the way.
He said save every coin you can; the more you hoard, the safer your next life.
chat.meaning: In AN 8.54 the Buddha gives Dighajanu four for this life, effort, protection, good friends and balanced living, and four for the next.

Dighajanu.meaning: a Koliyan layman who asked how to live well at home

Koliyan.meaning: of the Koliyas, a people of the Buddha's time

fig-eater.meaning: one who wastes wealth, shaking down a tree for a few figs

Nakula.meaning: the couple known as Nakula's parents, equal in four things

notes: AN 8.54 paraphrased. Confirm the list of occupations, the fig-tree (udumbara) simile and the 'starving man' simile.
Confirm the four drains (womanizing, drinking, gambling, bad friends); the script renders the first gender-neutrally as 'chasing other people's spouses'.
Confirm 'Dighajanu' = 'long-knee' and that Vyagghapajja is the clan name.
'Some call it the Buddha's financial advice' is a popular framing; a Keeper may prefer to drop it.
